title: Two-Way Tables
short: Use row and column totals to look for association in categorical data.

blocks.html: Some data are categories, not numbers: yes or no, 7th or 8th grade. A two-way table counts how many fall into each pair of categories. Reading it uses the same thinking as compound probability.

Counts can mislead when the groups have different sizes. If 30 of 50 seventh graders and 30 of 100 eighth graders play a sport, the counts match but the rates are very different: 60% and 30%. Comparing relative frequencies, the share within each group, puts the groups on equal footing.

Add row and column totals. To compare groups, divide each count by its row total (or column total) to get relative frequencies. If the groups’ percents differ a lot, there is an association between the two variables.

blocks.title: Use the totals
blocks.q: In the table, how many students in all play a sport, and how many 8th graders were surveyed?
steps: The column total for “Plays a sport” is $30 + 12 = 42$.
The row total for 8th grade is $12 + 28 = 40$.

blocks.title: Relative frequencies
blocks.q: What percent of 7th graders play a sport? Of 8th graders?

blocks.title: Is there an association?
blocks.q: Is grade level associated with playing a sport in this survey?
steps: 60% of 7th graders play, but only 30% of 8th graders.
The percents are far apart, so yes: in this group, 7th graders were more likely to play a sport.

blocks.html: Comparing counts instead of percents. “30 seventh graders play but only 12 eighth graders” sounds convincing, but the groups have different sizes. Always divide by the group total before comparing.
